description: Make a fist and read what is missing. Your Fist Test grades whether your finger tendons still glide their full route. Five mistakes keep fingers stiff and swollen long after they should have freed up. Here is the full-close line, the pulley system explained, and the gliding work that gives your hands back.

scenes.narration: Open your hand wide, fingers spread, every joint straight. Now close it into the tightest fist you own, slowly, and look at what actually happens. Do your fingertips roll all the way down and press into the base of your palm? Or does the fist stop early, fingers hovering, joints refusing the last stretch of the journey? Estimate the gap, in centimetres, between your fingertips and your palm at maximum honest effort, and check each finger, because one stiff traveller often hides among four good ones. Then open again and notice the second signal: how did the closing feel, smooth or rusty? That is your Fist Test. A fist is not a strength move. It is a travel measurement, a reading of how far your finger tendons can glide through their tunnels, and glide is the first thing injured or irritated fingers lose. Remember your gap and your stiffest finger. At the end, I grade them.

scenes.label: FINGERTIPS THAT REACH HOME
scenes.narration: Here is the line. Fingertips that press fully into the palm, all four, with a smooth close, mean your finger tendons own their full travel. A gap under two centimetres on the worst finger is the common pattern after a jam, a sprain, or a long season of heavy gripping: glide that is present but short, and usually accompanied by morning stiffness that melts as the day warms up. Beyond two centimetres, or a finger that moves noticeably worse than its neighbours, the travel is restricted enough to change how you grip everything, and other fingers start paying compensation taxes. Two qualifiers keep this honest. Hands are stiffer first thing in the morning and after cold, so grade yourself at the same time of day when you compare. And an old, painless limitation you have had for decades is a different story from a gap that is new or growing. Trends and neighbours: that is what this test really grades.
scenes.sub: full close: full glide - under 2 cm: short travel - 2+: restricted

scenes.narration: Your fingers have almost no muscle in them, a fact this channel will never let you forget. The engines live in your forearm, and their force reaches the fingers along tendons that glide back and forth through a series of tunnels, held against the bones by little ligament guides called PULLEYS. Making a full fist pulls several centimetres of tendon through that system. Now you can see what stiffness really is. Swelling thickens the tendon. Irritation roughens the tunnel. A finger rested in a splint for weeks lets the whole route quieten and stick. Any of these shortens the travel, and the fist, that humble party trick, reports the shortage to the centimetre. This is also why finger rehab is so specific: the goal is rarely strength first. The goal is glide, restoring the tendon's commute through its tunnels, because a tendon that cannot travel cannot be loaded properly anyway.

Hand therapists have a saying: motion is lotion. It sounds like a greeting card and it is actually the mechanism. Every gentle trip a tendon makes through its tunnel pumps fluid, discourages the sticky adhesions that form between tendon and tunnel wall, and reminds the whole system of its full route. This is why the correct first exercise for stiff fingers is almost offensively easy: slow, full-range opening and closing, fingertip touches, tendon-gliding positions, done often, at low effort. And it is why the instinct to squeeze a stress ball as hard as possible backfires so often: maximal gripping loads a system whose travel is already short, irritating the tunnels further. Sequence is everything here. First restore the commute, then strengthen the traveller. Glide daily, load gradually, and the fist closes like a door being re-hung on oiled hinges.

beats.text: TRACK THE CLOCK, NOT JUST THE GAP

scenes.narration: Add a second gauge beside the gap: the warm-up clock. How many minutes after waking do your hands take to feel like yours again? Healthy hands are ready in moments. Irritated tendon systems often need twenty minutes, a warm shower, and the first tasks of the day before the fingers move freely, and that number moves beautifully with healing, often before the fist gap does. Track both and you have a dashboard. One signal deserves its own sentence, because it changes the conversation: a finger that CATCHES, locks, or snaps painfully as it bends is describing a tendon struggling through one tight pulley, the pattern called trigger finger. Gliding work may still help it, but catching and locking are not ordinary stiffness, and they earn a professional assessment rather than a home experiment. Know which story your hand is telling.

lines: Your glide reps can be endless.
beats.title: THE SKINNY ADVANTAGE

scenes.narration: Your advantage is frequency, and in glide work frequency is everything. Tendon gliding costs nothing: no equipment, no recovery, no load budget spent. A heavier athlete's hands carry a day of serious gripping debt into every session, while yours arrive comparatively fresh, free to spend the day accumulating dozens of easy, full-range reps at your desk, in the car, during calls. Stiffness melts under exactly that pattern: many small trips through the full route, reminding the tunnels of their job. This is the one corner of rehab where the prescription reads like your natural habits anyway. Light hands, endless reps, zero drama. The guys with the crushing grips envy nothing about your hands today. In three months of gliding, they will envy the fist.
Now glide with me. Open wide, hook the fingers, roll to a fist, open again, slow and full. Forty seconds flowing, twenty to rest, three rounds. Easy effort. Go.

beats.text: 5. WAITING FOR IT TO FREE ITSELF

scenes.narration: The five mistakes that keep fingers stiff long after they should be free. One: splinting or resting the hand completely still for weeks beyond the early healing phase, which protects the injury and manufactures the stiffness. Two: attacking the stiffness with maximal squeezing, loading a short-travel system until the tunnels complain louder. Three: exercising only the good hand, because it feels productive, while the stiff one falls further behind. Four: ignoring the morning clock, the cheapest healing gauge you own. Five: waiting for it to free itself, when glide is restored by trips, not by time. The thread through all five is the same: travel returns to fingers that travel, a little, very often, at easy effort. And the standing line of this season: a finger that locks or triggers, swelling that does not settle, stiffness after a fracture or cut, or a gap that keeps growing, see a professional if it persists. Hands are too important to guess with.

scenes.label: THEN WE MAKE A FIST AGAIN
scenes.narration: So, your grade. A gap beyond two centimetres means a glide program: daily tendon glides, heat before sessions if mornings are rough, and patience measured in weeks while the travel returns. Under two centimetres is short travel, the most common grade here, and it responds beautifully to frequency: many easy trips, every day, no heroics. A full, smooth close means your system owns its route; keep it travelling and spend your training ambition on grip strength, in that order, forever. Watch the warm-up clock as your second opinion. When mornings free up faster, the tunnels are clearing, whatever the mirror says. Put your gap in the comments. Just the number. We make a fist again in thirty days.
scenes.sub: 2+ cm: glide program - under 2: short travel - full close: full glide

scenes.narration: Thirty days from now, same time of day, same slow fist, and we grade that travel again. Subscribe, because next we open the files on the most famous pain in the foot: the one waiting for you on the first step of the morning. This is {channel}. Train the cable.

title: 5 finger stiffness Mistakes That Are Destroying Your finger tendon healing
